newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia criticizes U.S. drug decision.
newsitem.headline: Colombia criticizes U.S. drug decision.

text.p: The Colombian government strongly criticised Washington's decision on Friday to keep it on a blacklist of countries deemed unreliable allies in the war on drugs.

Vice President Carlos Lemos Simmonds, who said the decision threatened to drive U.S.-Colombian relations to a new low, called it "arbitrary and unjust" and said the annual U.S. drug test known as "certification" had lost all credibility.

In a thinly veiled swipe at Mexico, which was certified as a worthy ally against drug-trafficking, Lemos said the entire certification process appeared based more on "political and commercial considerations" than on objective evidence of drug- fighting efforts.

Mexico was rocked by numerous drug-corruption scandals over the past year but many Colombians expected it to be certified, despite evidence of rampant corruption, because of its economic and geographical importance to the United States.
Countries that are "decertified" face potential economic or commercial sanctions.
"This decision will seriously harm the good relations that have always existed between Colombia and the United States," Lemos said in his statement, which was issued by the presidential palace.
"Entire decades of friendship, alliance and cooperation have been wiped out by a procedure lacking in any credibility."

Lemos said a steady increase in drug consumption in countries like the United States was the root cause of the drug problem in Colombia. "They can't become our judges or pretend to punish us for something that they are principally to blame for," he said.
Emilio Lebolo, head of the ruling Liberal Party, said Colombia was clearly being made the "scapegoat," however.
"The United States is failing in its own anti-drug fight so it was looking for a scapegoat," he said.

Fabio Valencia, head of the opposition Conservative Party, said the U.S. decision was expected because Washington repeatedly accused President Ernesto Samper of financing his 1994 election campaign with drug money.
"As long as President Samper remains in power the United States isn't going to certify Colombia's anti-drug fight," he said.
Colombia's Congress absolved Samper last year, three months after the country was decertified for the first time, of any wrongdoing in his campaign.
But U.S. drug czar Barry McCaffrey told Colombian reporters in Washington on Thursday that U.S. officials felt "continuing insecurity about President Samper and some of his accused officials."
